title: Diversification and the mix
blurb: Two kinds of risk, spreading out, and what a crash does to a mix.

levels.title: Two kinds of risk
learn: Say what happens to a mix when one company fails and when a whole market falls.
Tell which kind of risk owning more companies fixes.

cards.text: Maya has $10,000 and puts the same amount into each company she owns. Suppose one company goes bankrupt and what she put in it is lost. Each company gets $10,000 divided by the number of companies. The numbers are made up for this example.

That is company risk: the chance that one company does badly or fails, whatever the rest of the market does. A bankruptcy, a recall or a fire can cause it. Owning more companies shrinks it, because each one becomes a smaller slice of your money.

A different event. The whole Canadian market falls 20% and every other market stays flat. Dev owns 50 Canadian companies, $200 in each, $10,000 in all. All 50 fall together, so he loses 20% of $10,000, which is $2,000. Owning 50 companies did not help him.

That is market risk: the chance that a whole market falls and takes its companies down together. What lowers it is spreading across places that do not fall together. The same $10,000 is below with less of it in Canada. The loss is the share in Canada times 20%.

Spreading out has limits. If every market falls at once, no place stays flat and a mix still loses. It also does not raise what you can expect to earn. It narrows the range of results you might land in: fewer very bad years and fewer very good ones.

So there are two jobs. More companies shrink company risk. More places, and more kinds of companies, shrink market risk. A mix of 200 companies that are all in one country has done the first job and very little of the second.

levels.title: Four ways to spread
learn: Describe a company by its size, style, sector and country.
Read a mix to see where it is spread and where it is bunched.

cards.text: A mix can be spread out in four ways: by size, by style, by sector and by geography. A mix can be spread in one way and bunched in another. This level goes through the four, then reads a small mix.

Size is how big a company is: large or small. Style is how the market prices it. A growth company sells at a high price because buyers expect fast growth. A value company sells at a low price compared with what it earns. Nobody knows in advance which does better, so a mix may hold both.

A sector is a group of companies that do similar business. Four groups: interest sensitive (banks and others whose business moves with interest rates), consumer (sells to everyday shoppers), industrial (builds and moves things) and resources (oil, mines, forests).

Geography is where a company is based and does business: Canada, the United States, other countries (international) and emerging markets, which are countries whose markets are younger and growing fast. Companies in one country tend to rise and fall together.
Here is a made-up mix of five companies with $2,000 in each. Read it one way at a time: by sector, by size and by country.

Read by country: four of the five are in Canada, so the mix is bunched there. Read by size: four large and one small. Companies in the same sector also tend to fall together, so two bank shares count as two companies but move almost like one.

levels.title: What a fund holds
learn: Read the three facts that show what a fund holds.
Work out the share of a mix of funds that sits in one country.

cards.text: A fund is one purchase that holds many companies at once. Each company it holds is a holding. Three facts on its page say most: how many holdings it has, its largest sector and that sector's weight, and what share of its money sits in each country. A weight is a share of the money, as a percent.
Here are three made-up funds. Read the three facts off each row. No real fund is described.

Fund R has 200 holdings, so one company failing barely shows. But 97% of its money is in Canada. If Canada falls 20% and other markets stay flat, Fund R falls about 97% x 20%, which is 19.4%. Many holdings fix company risk. They do not fix market risk.

Is a fund of 200 Canadian companies diversified? Partly: it is spread across companies, not across countries. Funds can also be bunched in the same way. Two funds that are both mostly banks look like two holdings but move almost like one, because banks tend to fall together.

You can mix funds. The share of a mix in Canada is each fund's Canada share times its weight in your money, added up. Put 50% in Fund R and 50% in Fund S: 50% x 97% + 50% x 3% = 48.5% + 1.5% = 50%. Half of the money is in Canada.

Real funds show these numbers on their own pages, usually with a date. Write down the page and the date next to each number you copy, because what a fund holds can change. The numbers on these cards are made up.

levels.title: A blended return
learn: Work out the return of a mix from its parts and their weights.
Say what a REIT is and how its return is made.

cards.text: A mix has parts that earn different returns. Its blended return is worked out from each part and how much money is in it. It is not the middle of the returns. Picture a see-saw: the balance point sits closer to the end that holds more money.

Here is the class example, with made-up rates. The $10,000 earns $640 + $60 = $700 in a year, which is 7%. The stocks part holds most of the money, so the whole earns 7%, close to the stocks rate of 8%. The middle of 8% and 3% would be 5.5%, which is wrong.

figure.title: Stocks and cash, rates made up

cards.text: A shortcut gives the same answer, and it is the step you used to blend funds: weight times value, added up. Multiply each part's weight by its return and add. For 80% stocks at 8% and 20% cash at 3%: 80% x 8% + 20% x 3% = 6.4% + 0.6% = 7.0%. The weights add up to 100%. A mix never earns more than its best part.

Real estate can be a part of a mix. A REIT, a real estate investment trust, owns buildings that earn rent, such as apartments, warehouses and offices. You buy units like shares. It pays most of its rent out to its owners as distributions, often every month.

A REIT's return is its yield plus the change in the price of its units. The yield is the yearly payout as a percent of the price. The price can fall, so the payout is not the whole return. Here is a three-part mix with made-up rates.

figure.title: A three-part mix, rates made up

cards.text: For that mix: 50% x 8% + 30% x 4% + 20% x 6% = 4.0% + 1.2% + 1.2% = 6.4%. Check that the weights add up to 100% before you start. Moving money toward the part with the higher return raises the blend. The next level shows what that can cost.

levels.title: A crash hits the mix
learn: Work out how much a mix falls in a crash from its share in stocks.
Say what a mix with less in stocks gives up and keeps.

cards.text: Two investors each have $100,000. Investor A holds 80% in stocks and 20% in the steady part (GICs and bonds). Investor C holds 30% in stocks and 70% in the steady part. A bad year comes. Does each lose the same share of their money?
Here is a made-up crash, for this example only: stocks fall 30% and the steady part holds its value. Real crashes are different every time. The table shows each investor after the crash.

figure.title: After a made-up crash: stocks fall 30%

cards.text: Here is the rule. When the steady part holds, the whole mix falls by its share in stocks times the crash size. For A: 80% x 30% = 24%, so $100,000 falls to $76,000. For C: 30% x 30% = 9%, so $100,000 falls to $91,000.

The same crash does not cost every mix the same. A mix with half its money in stocks falls 15% here. One with more in stocks falls more, and one with less falls less. Look at how the whole mix falls for each share in stocks.

figure.title: How much the whole mix falls (stocks fall 30%)

cards.text: Two cautions. The 30% is made up. And the steady part is not always steady: bond funds can fall too, for example when interest rates rise. Then a real mix can lose more than this rule says. The rule shows how a mix's weights matter. It is not a forecast.

The game's Exchange has a fund, DAA Balanced 60/40, that holds 60% in its index fund and 40% in its bond fund. An index fund holds every company on a list, such as every company in town. In the same made-up crash the index part falls 30% and the bond part holds. These are not the game's own crash numbers.

traps.why: That is how far the index part falls. Only 60% of the fund is in it.

questions.miss: Multiply the index fund's weight by the size of the fall.

questions.label: Why C lost less
questions.prompt: In the made-up crash, why did Investor C lose less than Investor A?
questions.hint: Compare each investor's share in stocks.

options.text: C picked stocks that fell less
options.why: The stocks fell 30% for both investors.

options.text: Only 30% of C's money was in the part that fell
options.why: Yes. C had less of the money in stocks.

options.text: C's steady part gained value in the crash
options.why: In this example the steady part held its value. It did not gain.

questions.label: C's blended return
questions.prompt: In an ordinary year, in this example, stocks earn 8% and the steady part earns 3%. What is Investor C's blended return? C has 30% in stocks. Round to one decimal place.

terms.meaning: The return of a whole mix, worked out from the return of each part and how much money is in it.

questions.hint: Weight times return for each part, then add.

traps.why: That is the middle of 8% and 3%. C's weights are 30% and 70%.

questions.miss: Do 30% of 8% and 70% of 3%, then add.

questions.label: Ordinary year
questions.prompt: Investor A earns a blended return of 7.0% in an ordinary year, in this example. C lost less in the crash. In an ordinary year (stocks 8%, steady part 3%), how does C compare with A?
questions.hint: Work out each investor's blended return.

options.text: C earns a higher blended return than A
options.why: C holds less in stocks, the part with the higher rate, so C earns less in an ordinary year.

options.text: C earns the same blended return as A
options.why: The two mixes have different weights, so their blended returns differ.

options.text: C earns a lower blended return than A
options.why: Yes. C's 4.5% is lower than A's 7.0%. A smaller loss in a crash came with a lower return.

questions.label: Real bonds
questions.prompt: The card says bond funds can fall when interest rates rise. What does that mean for Investor A's made-up 24% fall?
questions.hint: Which part did the rule say would hold?

options.text: A real mix like A could lose more than 24%
options.why: Yes. If the steady part falls too, the whole mix falls more than the rule says.

options.text: A real mix like A could never lose more than 24%
options.why: The rule assumed the steady part holds. If it falls, the loss is bigger.

options.text: The steady part would gain, so A loses less
options.why: A rise in interest rates tends to lower bond fund prices, not raise them.
